name: AWS App Runner
oneLiner: Provisioned memory bills around the clock. vCPU only ticks while requests are actually being handled.
trap: No per-request charge and no scale to zero: you pause the service or keep paying for memory. Builds bill per minute, auto-deploy is a flat monthly fee, and App Runner closed to new customers on 30 April 2026.

name: Amazon WorkSpaces Applications (AppStream 2.0)
oneLiner: Always-On fleet instances bill by the hour with nobody streaming. On-Demand adds a cheaper stopped rate.
trap: A single Windows streaming session in a month makes that user liable for a whole RDS SAL fee, counted separately per Region and never pro-rated. Rocky Linux, RHEL and Windows BYOL fleets skip the user fee.

name: AWS Batch
oneLiner: Batch itself is free. The scheduler costs nothing; you pay only for the EC2, Fargate or Lambda it launches.
trap: Zero-cost scheduler that can start a lot of EC2 very fast. The real bill is compute environments whose min vCPUs never scale to zero between jobs.

name: AWS Compute Optimizer
oneLiner: Recommendations are free; only the optional enhanced infrastructure metrics bill, per resource per hour.
trap: Free until someone flips on enhanced infrastructure metrics, which then bills per resource-hour - and for Auto Scaling groups it charges per running EC2 instance, not per group.

name: Amazon EC2
oneLiner: Instance-seconds are the headline. EBS volumes and public IPv4 addresses ride along, and outbound bytes meter too.
trap: An auto-assigned public IPv4 is released when you stop the instance, so that charge stops; an Elastic IP keeps billing until released. The EBS volume bills either way. Cross-AZ traffic is metered on both ends.

name: Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling
oneLiner: Free. Auto Scaling has no charge of its own - you pay only for the instances it launches.
trap: The service is free, but the CloudWatch alarms and detailed monitoring that drive it are not, and every launch re-triggers the per-instance billing minimum.

name: Amazon EC2 Spot
oneLiner: The same instance-seconds as On-Demand, charged at the current Spot price. The discount is the difference.
trap: Your max price never changes what you pay - you always pay the Spot price in effect. If AWS interrupts you in the first hour it is free, but if YOU terminate you pay for the seconds used.

name: Amazon Elastic Container Registry
oneLiner: Storage per GB-month plus data transfer out. In-Region pulls to EC2, Fargate, Lambda and App Runner are free.
trap: Cross-Region replication charges data transfer out against the source Region on every copy. Untagged and superseded layers keep accruing storage until a lifecycle policy actually deletes them.

name: Amazon ECR Public
oneLiner: Storage past the always-free allowance, and internet bandwidth once the free limits run out.
trap: Publishing stays cheap because the puller pays. Past the free allowance, internet data transfer out of a public repo bills the AWS account doing the download, while storage stays on the repo owner.

name: Amazon ECS
oneLiner: Orchestration costs nothing. The bill is whatever EC2 or Fargate capacity your tasks land on.
trap: Free only holds for tasks on your own EC2 or on Fargate. ECS Anywhere bills per registered on-premises instance-hour, and ECS Managed Instances add a per-instance management fee on top of the EC2 rate.

name: Amazon EKS
oneLiner: Flat hourly fee per cluster for the control plane. Nodes and everything they touch are billed separately.
trap: An empty cluster still pays the hourly fee, and drifting into extended Kubernetes support multiplies it six times over. Cross-AZ pod traffic and NAT land on the EC2 and VPC bills, not on the EKS one.

name: Amazon EKS Anywhere
oneLiner: Free to run on your own hardware. The Enterprise Subscription bills per cluster for a fixed term.
trap: Subscription price is flat per cluster and ignores node count, so a three-node edge cluster costs what a large one costs. Past the first 7 days the 1-year or 3-year term cannot be cancelled.

name: AWS Elastic Beanstalk
oneLiner: A free wrapper. The bill is whatever EC2, load balancer and database resources the environment stands up.
trap: Beanstalk's own line item is always zero, so the cost hides under EC2 and ELB. A forgotten dev environment keeps paying for its load balancer and instances indefinitely.

name: AWS Fargate
oneLiner: Per-second billing on the vCPU and memory a task requests, not on what it uses.
trap: The meter starts at docker pull, not when your app comes up, and there is a one-minute minimum per task. Windows tasks carry a per-vCPU OS licence charge and a five-minute minimum instead.

name: AWS Lambda
oneLiner: Every invocation bills twice: once as a request, once as GB-seconds of memory multiplied by run time.
trap: Provisioned concurrency bills from the moment you enable it until you turn it off, with zero invocations. Since 1 August 2025 the INIT phase counts toward billed duration on on-demand invokes as well.

name: Amazon Lightsail
oneLiner: One flat bundle price per instance, with a monthly data-transfer allowance folded into it.
trap: A stopped instance keeps accruing the bundle rate until you delete it. Traffic in both directions eats the allowance, but only outbound past it is billed. A static IP left unattached bills by the hour.

name: AWS Outposts
oneLiner: A 3-year capacity commitment billed upfront and/or monthly, plus hourly fees for AWS services on it.
trap: Capacity is paid for whether you use it or not, and Enterprise Support is mandatory. Outpost-to-Region and Local Gateway traffic are free, but Region-to-Outpost is charged as normal data transfer out.

name: Amazon WorkDocs
oneLiner: Shut down. WorkDocs reached end of support on 25 April 2025 and the service is gone.
trap: The user guide has been withdrawn and the pricing offer is frozen at 2022. While it ran it billed per user-month, per GB stored and per API call — though deletes were rated at zero. Nothing to migrate to inside AWS.

name: Amazon WorkSpaces
oneLiner: AlwaysOn desktops pay a fixed monthly rate. AutoStop pays a smaller monthly base fee plus hourly usage.
trap: The monthly fee is pro-rated in the first month only, then charged in full even if nobody logs in. Flipping AutoStop to AlwaysOn mid-month overlaps both models, so AWS suggests doing it near month end.

name: Amazon WorkSpaces Secure Browser
oneLiner: Billed per monthly active user, not per running instance.
trap: A single sign-in during the calendar month makes that user billable in full; there is no partial MAU. Included streaming hours are granted per MAU, so heavy users tip into hourly overage while idle accounts cost nothing.
